tier_reason: The README (English and Japanese) carries first-party tables only: Cloudflare Workers authia 0.20/0.17/0.36 ms avg/p50/p95 vs jose (WebCrypto) 0.30/0.28/0.50 ms, and Node.js jose 0.01-0.03 ms vs authia 0.17-0.20 ms. No harness, CPU, runtime versions, jose version or iteration counts are published; benches/ holds only Rust criterion benches of authia itself (jwt_split, verify_token_legacy_base64, verify_token_raw_jwk), never jose.

corrections.caveats: Mixed, first-party result: the README says jose is significantly faster on Node.js (native crypto, 0.01-0.03 ms vs authia 0.17-0.20 ms, 6-20x slower, derived from page data) and recommends jose for Node backends and for production systems requiring maximum stability. The only win is about 1.5x on Cloudflare Workers, where both use similar APIs. The jose comparison harness is not in the repository: benches/ (jwt_verify.rs, jwt_verify_real.rs) contains Rust criterion benches of authia alone, and examples/ holds usage samples only. No CPU, Workers/wrangler or Node versions, jose version or iteration counts are stated; Cloudflare Workers freezes Date.now()/performance.now() during synchronous execution, so how the sub-millisecond per-call Workers times were taken is unclear. README Known Issues: v0.3.1-v0.3.3 strict claim schema can reject tokens missing optional fields such as email. Repository has 3 commits; package.json and Cargo.toml still point to Taniyama2024/authia (moved to HaradaTakuma/authia).

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; tier C stands (first-party, no methodology, no published jose harness). Shortcomings to record: slower than jose on Node.js by 6-20x, Workers-only 1.5x win, no benchmark code against jose, 0 stars and 3 commits.

tier_reason: README Performance Profiling section gives the author's own browser-benchmark result (JS 600 points in 16 ms vs Rust/wasm same workload in 8.165 ms, 1.95x; 1220 points in 16 ms) against a port of d3-geo-voronoi's benchmark page; benchmark code is public (benchmark/) but no CPU, browser, Rust flags or run counts are stated, so C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 8 stars, 1 fork; crates.io d3_geo_voronoi_rs 43,266 downloads (375 recent), version 0.10.7
corrections.compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack via webpack (@wasm-tool/wasm-pack-plugin), 'npm run build' (webpack.production.config.js) in benchmark/; workspace release profile lto = true, codegen-units = 1; no rustc version or target-feature flags stated
corrections.caveats: Single author measurement with no CPU, browser, run counts or variance. The 8.165 ms / 1.95x figures were written in the README on 2023-08-20 (commit b8979d0 'Update performance report'; before that the README said 11 ms, a 31% speedup) and have not been re-measured for the current 0.10.x code. The benchmark renders a Delaunay mesh to canvas each frame, so the comparison covers the whole pipeline (Rust ports of d3-geo and d3-delaunay plus canvas drawing), not just the Voronoi step. README build instructions point to benchmark/www, which no longer exists (package.json now sits in benchmark/), and to d3-geo-voronoi src/benchmark/sphereCanvas.html, whereas the JS repo's benchmark is now in a top-level benchmark/ directory. README notes a failing test ('geoVoronoi.hull does not break on difficult polygons') and that the demo only works with f64 (f32 breaks cell integrity). Licence is MIT only via Cargo.toml (workspace.package license = "MIT"); the repository has no LICENSE file. Workspace patches geo/geo-types to the author's own git branch and delaunator to its unpublished master.

notes: Numbers match the README; tier C stands. Shortcomings to record: no hardware or browser stated, numbers from 2023 not re-measured, whole-pipeline including canvas rendering, no LICENSE file (MIT declared in Cargo.toml), failing hull test, stale build instructions.

reject_reason: other: fabricated or illustrative numbers presented as benchmark results (README table written before any JS benchmark existed; BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md is self-labelled 'Sample' and cannot be output of the repo's own harness)
tier_reason: No measured numbers survive: the README Performance table (2.3 vs 0.6 ms, 8.7 vs 2.1 ms, 15.2 vs 0.8 ms) already appears in the initial implementation commit a1ef085 (2025-10-22), which adds only a Rust criterion bench (benches/performance.rs) and no JavaScript benchmark; BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md was added in one AI-co-authored commit (ab26a59, 2025-10-22) together with benchmarks/comparison.js and is internally inconsistent with that harness.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: npm run bench:all = 'npm run build:nodejs' then 'node benchmarks/comparison.js' (tinybench, 1000 iterations, 100 warmup); build:nodejs is 'wasm-pack build --target nodejs' at ab26a59 but 'wasm-pack build --dev --target nodejs' (an unoptimised debug build) in the current package.json; no Rust or wasm-opt flags stated
corrections.hardware: BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md names Apple M1 Max (Node v20.11.0) and Intel i7-12700K (Node v20.11.0) with results, and a 2-core GitHub Actions Xeon with no results; all dated 2025-01-22, nine months before the repository's first implementation commit (2025-10-22)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; crates.io orlando-transducers 44 downloads (created 2026-03-10); npm orlando-transducers
corrections.caveats: Evidence judged fabricated or illustrative, not measured. (1) The README Performance table (3.8x, 4.1x, 19x) is present in the initial implementation commit a1ef085 (co-authored by Claude Code), which contains no JavaScript benchmark at all; the JS harness benchmarks/comparison.js arrived later in commit ab26a59. (2) BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md calls itself 'Sample benchmark results', is dated 2025-01-22 although the code was first committed 2025-10-22 (the CHANGELOG shows the same year-month drift, 0.1.0 dated 2025-01-23), lists a third environment with no results, and tells readers to clone 'github.com/yourusername/orlando.git'. (3) In every row Ops/sec x Avg Time equals 10,000 (e.g. 18,234 ops/s and 0.55 ms; 24,391 and 0.41 ms), which matches no real timing (1 / 18,234 s is 0.055 ms) and not the harness either: comparison.js prints tinybench hz with up to two decimals and the mean multiplied by 1000 as 'ms', so a real run of it would show about 54.84 ms for 18,234 ops/s and ops x time near 1,000,000. (4) The harness times data.slice() of the full input inside every call for every library. (5) Even taken at face value the win is algorithmic (lazy single pass, early termination): pure-JS Lazy.js is within 1.1-1.2x of Orlando in every scenario and Orlando is 1.3-1.4x slower than native on a simple map. The current build:nodejs script builds wasm with --dev. Repository moved from justinelliottcobb/Orlando (package.json still points there); licence Apache-2.0 since v0.6.0.

notes: Reject for invalid evidence (r8e precedent: unmeasured figures presented as measurements): README speedups predate any JS benchmark code, and the 'Sample' results file has a constant ops x time product of 10,000 that neither real timing nor comparison.js output can produce. If the orchestrator prefers keep-and-document, it is tier D with the same shortcomings; the benchmark code itself is real and could be run.
